metadata.title: Claude, K12 Lesson Differentiation.
metadata.subtitle: The K12 Lesson Differentiation Skill
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: does differentiating a lesson for three reading levels mean writing three separate lessons? It doesn't — Claude tiers one shared lesson three ways from a single material-source file, so the versions can't drift apart. Lands the carry-out that the three tiers stay consistent because they render from one shared source, not three independent drafts.

beats.narration_text: Someone wonders if tiering a lesson for three levels means writing it separately. It doesn't — one lesson, tiered three ways. So: when Claude tiers a lesson for three levels, does it write one shared version?

beats.narration_text: A Skill is a folder Claude reads before it works. This one is called k12-lesson-differentiation. Its SKILL.md file holds the full instruction set, in plain language — no hidden logic. Claude reads it, then acts. The file is the program.
The instructions live in a Steps section. Claude reads each step in order and executes it — read the file, execute each step, return the result. Linear: no branching, unless a step says otherwise.

production_viz.label: READ, EXECUTE, RETURN
production_viz.caption: linear — no branching unless a step says so

beats.narration_text: One design choice matters most: all three tiers, and the teacher's own plan, render from a single material-source file. The facts get written once. Change a number in the source and every tier updates together — nothing to accidentally drift between the below-level version and the above-level version.
Claude isn't writing three different lessons — it's tiering one shared lesson three ways, from a single source file, so the three versions can't drift apart.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: I have a fifth grade fractions lesson, and my students read at three different levels. Read the k12-lesson-differentiation skill, and before you build anything, walk me through what you'll produce and how the tiers will stay consistent with each other.
